clinicalPearls: Coloboma results from failure of the embryonic optic (choroidal) fissure to close, so defects lie in a characteristic inferonasal distribution.
The malformations form a continuum: isolated iris coloboma, chorioretinal and optic disc coloboma, microphthalmia (a small but structured eye) and anophthalmia (a clinically absent eye).
Visual prognosis depends chiefly on whether the macula and optic nerve are involved; an iris coloboma alone producing a keyhole pupil may spare vision.
A substantial proportion are syndromic; CHARGE association (CHD7) is the classic link, while SOX2 and OTX2 are leading causes of anophthalmia and severe microphthalmia.
Chorioretinal colobomas carry a lifelong risk of retinal detachment through the thinned coloboma bed.
Severe microphthalmia and anophthalmia require early orbital conformers and expanders to stimulate orbital and mid-facial growth.
Bilateral disease and midline brain or pituitary anomalies (SOX2, OTX2) mandate neuro-imaging and endocrine review.
A colobomatous keyhole iris should prompt a search for posterior segment and systemic involvement rather than being dismissed as cosmetic.
reference.pathophysiology: During early embryonic development the optic vesicle invaginates to form the optic cup, and the choroidal (optic) fissure on its inferonasal aspect must fuse. Failure of this fusion produces coloboma, which characteristically affects the structures lying along the fissure line, namely the iris, ciliary body, retina and choroid and the optic disc, in an inferonasal distribution. Disruption of the transcriptional network that governs ocular morphogenesis, including SOX2, OTX2, PAX6, RAX and downstream regulators, at earlier stages arrests growth of the globe to produce microphthalmia, or prevents optic vesicle formation altogether to produce anophthalmia; the three phenotypes therefore represent a graded severity of the same developmental programme. Environmental insults such as maternal vitamin A deficiency or excess, gestational infection or teratogen exposure can phenocopy the genetic forms, and inheritance in familial disease is most often autosomal dominant with marked variable expressivity.
additionalDifferentials: CHARGE syndrome (coloboma, heart defects, choanal atresia, growth retardation, genital and ear anomalies)
Congenital infection with chorioretinal scarring mimicking chorioretinal coloboma
Retinoblastoma or other cause of leukocoria when microphthalmia has an intraocular mass
Persistent fetal vasculature (persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous)
Morning glory disc anomaly, distinct from a true optic disc coloboma
Isolated congenital cataract and anterior segment dysgenesis
additionalInvestigations: Detailed dilated fundus examination and slit-lamp assessment of both eyes
Ocular biometry and B-scan ultrasound to document axial length in microphthalmia
Orbital and neuro-imaging (MRI) of optic nerves, chiasm, pituitary and brain
Chromosomal microarray with a targeted gene panel (SOX2, OTX2, PAX6, CHD7 and others)
Systemic evaluation for CHARGE including echocardiography, hearing assessment and endocrine review
Examination of parents and relatives for subtle iris coloboma in dominant families
redFlags: Sudden visual loss or a new field defect indicating retinal detachment through a chorioretinal coloboma
Leukocoria that may represent retinoblastoma rather than coloboma
Cyanosis or feeding difficulty from choanal atresia suggesting CHARGE association
Midline brain or pituitary anomaly with hypopituitarism in SOX2 or OTX2 disease
reference.prognosis: Visual outcome ranges from normal in isolated iris coloboma to severe bilateral impairment with macular or optic nerve coloboma and with anophthalmia. Overall systemic prognosis is governed by any underlying syndrome rather than by the eye malformation alone.
pitfalls: Assuming an isolated eye finding when it is the presenting sign of a syndrome, so failing to screen for CHARGE or midline defects.
Mistaking a chorioretinal coloboma for old chorioretinitis scarring.
Under-recognising the lifelong risk of retinal detachment.
Forgetting early socket expansion with conformers in infants with anophthalmia, which is needed to promote orbital and facial growth.
Neglecting amblyopia therapy in unilateral cases with useful residual vision.
